meta.book_title: metricsAI: An Introduction to Econometrics with Python and AI in the Cloud

practice.concept: Standard error of the slope (Sections 7.1–7.2)
practice.stem: Suppose a regression of hourly wages on years of education for 100 workers gives a slope of b₂ = 5.2 with a standard error of 1.8. What does the 1.8 describe?

options.text: How much individual workers' hourly wages typically differ from the average wage in the sample
options.feedback: That is the standard deviation of wages, a feature of the data. The standard error belongs to the slope estimate and describes its uncertainty.

options.text: How much the years of education vary across the 100 workers
options.feedback: That is the spread of the explanatory variable (a standard deviation of x), which is an ingredient of the standard error but not the standard error itself.

options.text: How much the slope estimate would typically vary across random samples of 100 workers
options.feedback: Correct. The standard error measures the sampling variability of b₂: how much it would change from one random sample to another.

options.text: The predicted hourly wage of a worker with zero years of education
options.feedback: That is the intercept of the fitted line. The standard error is a measure of uncertainty attached to the slope.

practice.explanation: Section 7.2: a standard deviation describes the spread of the data; a standard error describes how much an estimate would vary across repeated samples. Here, b₂ = 5.2 would typically move by about 1.8 from sample to sample.

practice.concept: Sample estimate vs. population parameter (Sections 7.1–7.2)
practice.stem: Suppose the researcher in the wage study draws a second random sample of 100 different workers from the same population and re-estimates the slope. What is most likely to happen?

options.text: It will differ somewhat from 5.2, since each sample gives a different estimate.
options.feedback: Correct. b₂ is computed from a sample, so it changes from sample to sample; both estimates are attempts to learn the same population slope β₂.

options.text: It will be exactly 5.2, since both samples come from the same population.
options.feedback: Two samples from the same population still contain different workers, so the estimates differ. That sampling variation is what the standard error measures.

options.text: It will equal the population slope β₂, since a second sample removes the error.
options.feedback: A second sample is just another sample: its estimate also contains sampling error. No single sample reveals β₂ exactly.

options.text: It is certain to fall between 3.4 and 7.0, since the standard error is 1.8.
options.feedback: The standard error is a typical amount of variation, not a hard bound; estimates more than one standard error away from 5.2 are quite possible.

practice.explanation: Sections 7.1–7.2: b₂ is the sample estimate and β₂ the unknown population slope. Because b₂ varies from sample to sample, we need standard errors, confidence intervals, and tests to learn about β₂.

practice.concept: The t-distribution and degrees of freedom (Section 7.2, Key Concept 7.1)
practice.stem: In the chapter's notation, sₑ is the square root of Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)² / (n − 2), computed from the residuals. What does sₑ estimate?

options.text: The standard deviation σᵤ of the error term u
options.feedback: Correct. σᵤ is unknown, so it is estimated by sₑ, computed from the residuals.

options.text: The standard error of the slope estimate b₂
options.feedback: sₑ is an ingredient of se(b₂), but se(b₂) also divides by the spread of x: se(b₂) = sₑ / √Σ(xᵢ − x̄)².

options.text: The standard deviation of the explanatory variable x
options.feedback: The formula uses the residuals yᵢ − ŷᵢ, which measure distances of y from the fitted line, not the spread of x.

options.text: The standard deviation of y around its own mean ȳ
options.feedback: That would use deviations from ȳ. sₑ uses deviations from the fitted values ŷᵢ, so it measures scatter around the regression line.

practice.explanation: Section 7.2: sₑ² = Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)²/(n − 2) uses deviations from the fitted line, so sₑ estimates the spread of the error term u.

practice.concept: Degrees of freedom (Section 7.2, Key Concept 7.1)
practice.stem: Suppose a bivariate regression of wages on education is estimated with n = 100 workers. How many degrees of freedom does the t-distribution for the slope have?

options.feedback: Each estimated parameter uses up one degree of freedom, so the count is below n.
n − 1 applies when one parameter (such as a mean) is estimated. A bivariate regression estimates two: the intercept and the slope.
2 is the number of estimated parameters. Degrees of freedom are what remain: n minus that number.
Correct: n − 2 = 100 − 2 = 98, because the intercept and the slope are both estimated.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 7.1: a bivariate regression estimates two parameters (β₁ and β₂), so the t-distribution for the slope has n − 2 degrees of freedom.

practice.concept: The t-distribution vs. the normal distribution (Section 7.3, Key Concept 7.1)
practice.stem: As the degrees of freedom increase, the t-distribution gets closer and closer to the standard normal distribution.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. With more data, sₑ estimates σᵤ more reliably, the extra uncertainty shrinks, and t critical values approach the normal value 1.96.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit the table comparing t and z critical values in Section 7.3: look at what happens as the sample size grows.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 7.1: the t-distribution converges to the normal distribution as the sample size increases; the 95% critical value falls from 3.182 (3 df) to 2.306 (8 df) to 1.984 (98 df), toward 1.96.

practice.concept: What determines the standard error of the slope (Section 7.2)
practice.stem: Suppose a wage–education regression is re-run under different conditions. Which changes would, other things equal, make the standard error of the slope larger? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Using only 25 workers instead of 100
options.feedback: Correct: fewer observations mean less information, so the standard error rises (quartering n roughly doubles it).

options.text: Adding $2 to every worker's hourly wage
options.feedback: Shifting every y value by the same amount moves the line up but leaves the slope and the scatter around the line unchanged, so the standard error does not change.

options.text: Sampling workers whose education is concentrated between 12 and 13 years
options.feedback: Correct: little spread in x gives little information about the slope, so the standard error rises.

options.text: Wages that scatter more widely around the fitted line
options.feedback: Correct: more unexplained variation (larger sₑ) makes the slope less precise.

options.text: Testing H₀: β₂ = 3 instead of H₀: β₂ = 0
options.feedback: The null value changes the t statistic, not the standard error, which is computed before any null value is chosen.

practice.explanation: Section 7.2: se(b₂) = sₑ / √Σ(xᵢ − x̄)². It rises with more scatter around the line, fewer observations, and less spread in x. Shifting y or changing the null value leaves it unchanged.

practice.concept: Standard error formula (Section 7.2)
practice.stem: Suppose sₑ = 12, n = 36, and the standard deviation of x is 2. Using the shortcut se(b₂) ≈ sₑ / (√n × sₓ), what is the approximate standard error of the slope?

options.feedback: This is 12 ÷ 2: the sample size was left out. Divide by √36 = 6 as well.
This divides by n × sₓ = 72. The shortcut uses the square root of n.
This is 12 ÷ 6: the spread of x was left out. More spread in x lowers the standard error.

practice.explanation: se(b₂) ≈ sₑ / (√n × sₓ) = 12 / (6 × 2) = 1.0. Because n enters through its square root, quadrupling n halves the standard error.

practice.concept: Constructing a confidence interval (Section 7.3)
practice.stem: Suppose the wage–education slope is b₂ = 5.2 with se(b₂) = 1.8, and the critical value is about 2.0. What is the approximate 95% confidence interval for β₂?

options.feedback: This is 5.2 ± 1.8: the standard error was not multiplied by the critical value.
This is 5.2 ± 2.0: the critical value was used without multiplying it by the standard error.
This adds and subtracts 7.2, the full width of the interval. The margin of error is half the width: 2.0 × 1.8 = 3.6.

practice.explanation: Section 7.3: CI = b₂ ± t-critical × se(b₂) = 5.2 ± 2.0 × 1.8 = [1.6, 8.8]. The margin of error, 3.6, is the half-width of the interval.

practice.concept: Interpreting confidence intervals (Section 7.3, Key Concept 7.2)
practice.stem: A 95% confidence interval of [1.6, 8.8] for the wage–education slope means there is a 95% probability that the true slope β₂ lies between 1.6 and 8.8.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Key Concept 7.2 lists this as the classic misconception: β₂ is fixed, so a computed interval either contains it or not. The 95% describes the procedure.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. The 95% is the long-run success rate of the method: across repeated samples, about 95% of intervals built this way contain β₂.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 7.2: 'If we repeated the sampling process many times, 95% of the constructed intervals would contain β₂.' The randomness is in the sample, not in the parameter.

practice.concept: Width of confidence intervals (Section 7.3, Key Concept 7.2)
practice.stem: Which changes would make a confidence interval for the wage–education slope narrower, other things equal? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Collecting data on 400 workers instead of 100
options.feedback: Correct: a larger sample shrinks the standard error (and slightly lowers the critical value), so the interval narrows.

options.text: Switching from a 95% to a 99% confidence level
options.feedback: Higher confidence requires a larger critical value, so the interval gets wider, not narrower.

options.text: Testing whether β₂ = 6 instead of whether β₂ = 0
options.feedback: A confidence interval does not depend on any null value; it is built from b₂, its standard error, and the critical value.

options.text: Switching from a 95% to a 90% confidence level
options.feedback: Correct: lower confidence uses a smaller critical value, so the interval is narrower (the price is less confidence).

practice.explanation: Section 7.3: width = 2 × t-critical × se(b₂). The interval narrows with a lower confidence level, a larger sample, or less scatter around the line.

practice.concept: Margin of error and standard error (Section 7.3)
practice.stem: Suppose a 95% confidence interval for a slope is [1.6, 8.8], built as b₂ ± 2.0 × se(b₂). What is se(b₂)?

options.feedback: 3.6 is the margin of error (half the width). The standard error is the margin divided by the critical value 2.0.
Correct: the half-width is (8.8 − 1.6) ÷ 2 = 3.6, and 3.6 ÷ 2.0 = 1.8.
7.2 is the full width of the interval, which is twice the margin of error.
5.2 is the center of the interval, the point estimate b₂.

practice.explanation: The center of the interval is b₂ = 5.2 and the half-width (margin of error) is 3.6 = 2.0 × se(b₂), so se(b₂) = 1.8.

practice.concept: Comparing confidence intervals (Section 7.3, Key Concept 7.2)
practice.stem: Suppose two studies estimate the same slope. Study A reports a 95% confidence interval of [2, 4]; Study B reports [−1, 7]. Both are centered on 3. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: Study B's interval includes zero, so its slope is not significant at the 5% level.
options.feedback: Correct. A value inside the 95% interval is not rejected at the 5% level, and zero lies inside B's interval.

options.text: Study B's slope is economically more important, because its interval reaches 7.
options.feedback: Both estimates equal 3; the upper limit reflects uncertainty, not a larger effect.

options.text: Study A's slope is significant only because it uses a larger sample.
options.feedback: No sample sizes are given; A is significant because its whole interval lies above zero.

options.text: Study A's slope is not significant, because its interval is so narrow.
options.feedback: A narrow interval that excludes zero is strong evidence that the slope differs from zero, not evidence against significance.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 7.2: a 95% interval contains exactly the null values that a 5% two-sided test would not reject. B includes 0, so its slope is not significant at 5%; A's interval excludes 0.

practice.concept: Confidence intervals in small samples (Section 7.3, Key Concept 7.1)
practice.stem: Suppose two regressions have the same slope estimate and the same standard error, but one uses n = 4 observations (critical value 4.303) and the other n = 52 (critical value 2.009). Which 95% interval is wider?

options.text: The n = 52 interval, because more observations add uncertainty
options.feedback: More observations reduce uncertainty. With equal standard errors, only the critical value differs, and it is larger for the small sample.

options.text: Neither, because the two standard errors are equal
options.feedback: The margin of error is critical value × standard error, so equal standard errors still give different widths when the critical values differ.

options.text: It cannot be determined without the slope estimate
options.feedback: The slope estimate sets the center of the interval, not its width.

options.text: The n = 4 interval, because its critical value is larger
options.feedback: Correct: with only 2 degrees of freedom the critical value is 4.303, so the margin is more than twice as large as with 2.009.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 7.1: with few degrees of freedom, the t-distribution's heavy tails produce large critical values and wide intervals. Width = 2 × t-critical × se(b₂).

practice.concept: Interpreting p-values (Section 7.4, Key Concept 7.3)
practice.stem: Suppose a regression of crop yield on fertilizer gives a slope of 1.5, and the test of H₀: β₂ = 0 gives a two-sided p-value of 0.03. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: There is a 97% probability that adding fertilizer truly raises crop yields on average.
options.feedback: A p-value is not the probability that a hypothesis is true or false; it is computed assuming H₀ is true.

options.text: If the true slope were 1.5, an estimate this far from zero would occur in about 3% of samples.
options.feedback: The p-value is computed assuming H₀ (β₂ = 0) is true, not assuming the true slope equals the estimate.

options.text: If the study were repeated on new farms, there is a 97% chance it would again find a significant slope.
options.feedback: The p-value is not a replication probability; it describes how surprising the estimate would be if β₂ were 0.

options.text: If β₂ were 0, an estimate as far from zero as 1.5, or farther, would occur in about 3% of samples.
options.feedback: Correct. The p-value is the probability, assuming H₀ is true, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 7.3: the p-value is the probability of observing a result at least as extreme as ours if H₀ is true. A small p-value is evidence against H₀, not the probability that H₀ is true.

practice.concept: Tests of statistical significance (Section 7.4)
practice.stem: In the wage–education regression (b₂ = 5.2, se(b₂) = 1.8, n = 100), the two-sided critical values are about 1.98 at the 5% level and 2.63 at the 1% level. What do you conclude about H₀: β₂ = 0?

options.text: Reject H₀ at the 5% level but not at the 1% level
options.feedback: t = 5.2 ÷ 1.8 ≈ 2.89, which also exceeds the 1% critical value of 2.63.

options.text: Reject H₀ at neither level
options.feedback: t = 5.2 ÷ 1.8 ≈ 2.89, well above 1.98 and above 2.63.

options.text: Reject H₀ at both the 5% and the 1% level
options.feedback: Correct: t = 5.2 ÷ 1.8 ≈ 2.89 exceeds both 1.98 and 2.63.

options.text: No decision is possible without the p-value
options.feedback: The critical-value approach and the p-value approach always give the same decision, so comparing |t| with the critical values is enough.

practice.explanation: Section 7.4: t = b₂ / se(b₂) = 5.2 / 1.8 ≈ 2.89. Reject H₀ at level α when |t| exceeds the critical value; 2.89 > 2.63 > 1.98, so H₀ is rejected at both levels.

practice.concept: The hypothesis testing framework (Section 7.4, Key Concept 7.3)
practice.stem: Which statements about hypothesis testing are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: With α = 0.01, a p-value of 0.03 is small enough to lead to rejecting H₀.
options.feedback: Reject only when p < α. Here 0.03 is above 0.01, so H₀ is not rejected at the 1% level.

options.text: Failing to reject H₀ means the evidence is insufficient, not that H₀ is proven.
options.feedback: Correct: we never 'accept' H₀; other values may be just as consistent with the data.

options.text: The p-value approach and the critical-value approach always reach the same decision.
options.feedback: Correct: p < α exactly when |t| exceeds the critical value.

options.text: α is the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
options.feedback: α is the probability of rejecting H₀ when H₀ is true (a Type I error), chosen before the test.

options.text: A smaller p-value indicates stronger evidence against H₀.
options.feedback: Correct: the less likely the result would be under H₀, the stronger the evidence against it.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 7.3: choose α (the Type I error probability), compute t and the p-value, and reject H₀ if p < α (equivalently, |t| > critical value). Failing to reject is not proof of H₀.

practice.concept: Economic magnitude of the slope (Section 7.4, Key Concept 7.4)
practice.stem: With a wage–education slope of $5.20 per hour per year of education, how much higher is the predicted hourly wage of a worker with 4 more years of education?

options.feedback: Correct: 4 × $5.20 = $20.80 per hour.
This divides the slope by 4. The slope is the change per year, so multiply by the number of years.
This adds 4 to the slope. The predicted difference is the slope times the difference in years.
This multiplies the standard error (1.8) by 4. The economic magnitude comes from the slope estimate.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 7.4: economic significance is judged from the magnitude of b₂. Four more years of education predict 4 × 5.20 = $20.80 more per hour, a large difference.

practice.concept: Statistical vs. economic significance (Section 7.4, Key Concept 7.4)
practice.stem: Suppose a job-training program raises wages by $0.50 per hour (p = 0.001), about $1,000 per year for a full-time worker, and costs $10,000 per participant. Which assessment fits the chapter?

options.text: The effect is large, because p = 0.001 signals a big effect.
options.feedback: A small p-value shows that the effect is distinguishable from zero, not that it is large.

options.text: The effect is significant, but it looks small relative to the cost.
options.feedback: Correct: statistically significant, but $1,000 a year against a $10,000 cost makes its economic value questionable.

options.text: The effect is not real, because $0.50 per hour is a small number.
options.feedback: A small effect can still be real; p = 0.001 is strong evidence that it differs from zero.

options.text: The effect is important, because any significant effect pays off.
options.feedback: Statistical significance says nothing about costs and benefits; that is the question of economic significance.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 7.4: statistical significance asks whether an effect differs from zero; economic significance asks whether it is large enough to matter. $0.50 × 2,000 hours = $1,000 a year may not justify a $10,000 program.

practice.concept: Sample size and significance (Section 7.4, Key Concept 7.4)
practice.stem: Suppose Regression A (n = 50) and Regression B (n = 10,000) both estimate a slope of 0.05, with standard errors of 0.10 and 0.01. Why is B's slope statistically significant while A's is not?

options.text: B's slope is larger in economic terms, since B uses far more observations.
options.feedback: Both slopes are 0.05, so their economic magnitude is the same.

options.text: A is tested at a stricter significance level, since its sample is smaller.
options.feedback: Nothing in the setup changes α; the difference comes from the standard errors.

options.text: B's smaller standard error puts the same 0.05 farther from zero in SE units.
options.feedback: Correct: t = 0.05 ÷ 0.01 = 5 for B but 0.05 ÷ 0.10 = 0.5 for A.

options.text: A's population slope must be negative, since its estimate is not significant.
options.feedback: Failing to reject H₀ says nothing about the sign of the population slope; A's estimate is positive too.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 7.4: with large n, the standard error shrinks and even small effects become statistically significant. Same coefficient, t = 0.5 versus t = 5.

practice.concept: Statistical vs. economic significance (Section 7.4, Key Concept 7.4)
practice.stem: If a slope is statistically significant at the 1% level, it must be large enough to matter in economic terms.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit Key Concept 7.4: with a large enough sample, even a trivial effect can be statistically significant.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. Statistical significance only says the effect differs from zero; whether it matters depends on its size and context.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 7.4: statistical and economic significance can diverge. Always report the coefficient (magnitude) together with its standard error or confidence interval (precision).

practice.concept: Two-sided test of a specific value (Section 7.5)
practice.stem: A researcher claims that each year of education raises wages by exactly $6.00 per hour. With b₂ = 5.2 and se(b₂) = 1.8, what is the t statistic for H₀: β₂ = 6 against Hₐ: β₂ ≠ 6?

options.feedback: This is the difference 5.2 − 6 without dividing by the standard error.
This is the t statistic for H₀: β₂ = 0. Here the null value is 6.
This divides the difference by the null value 6. The t statistic divides by the standard error.
Correct: t = (5.2 − 6) ÷ 1.8 ≈ −0.44, far inside ±2, so the claim is not rejected.

practice.explanation: Section 7.5: t = (b₂ − β₂*) / se(b₂) = (5.2 − 6) / 1.8 ≈ −0.44. The claim of $6.00 is consistent with the data at the 5% level.

practice.concept: Confidence intervals and two-sided tests (Section 7.5, Key Concept 7.2)
practice.stem: The 95% confidence interval for the wage–education slope is [1.6, 8.8]. For which hypothesized values c would a two-sided test of H₀: β₂ = c be rejected at the 5% level? (Select all that apply.)

options.feedback: 2.0 lies inside [1.6, 8.8], so it is a plausible value and is not rejected.
Correct: 0 lies outside the interval, so H₀: β₂ = 0 is rejected at the 5% level.
6.0 lies inside the interval, so it is not rejected.
Correct: 9.5 lies above the upper limit 8.8, so it is rejected.

practice.explanation: Section 7.5: a two-sided test at 5% rejects H₀: β₂ = c exactly when c lies outside the 95% confidence interval.

practice.concept: Confidence intervals and two-sided tests (Section 7.5, Key Concept 7.2)
practice.stem: If a hypothesized value of β₂ lies inside the 95% confidence interval, a two-sided test of that value at the 5% level will not reject it.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. The 95% interval is the set of null values that a 5% two-sided test does not reject.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit 'Relationship to confidence intervals' in Section 7.5.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 7.2 and Section 7.5: if β₂* falls inside the 95% CI, we fail to reject H₀: β₂ = β₂* at the 5% level; if it falls outside, we reject.

practice.concept: Setting up one-sided hypotheses (Section 7.6, Key Concept 7.5)
practice.stem: In a regression of sales (in millions of dollars) on advertising (in thousands of dollars), a colleague claims the slope exceeds 5, that is, β₂ > 5. Which pair of hypotheses tests this claim?

options.text: H₀: β₂ > 5 against Hₐ: β₂ ≤ 5
options.feedback: The claim we want to support goes in the alternative hypothesis, not the null.

options.text: H₀: β₂ ≤ 5 against Hₐ: β₂ > 5
options.feedback: Correct: the claim becomes Hₐ, and the null is its opposite. This is an upper-tailed test.

options.text: H₀: β₂ ≥ 5 against Hₐ: β₂ < 5
options.feedback: This tests the opposite claim, that the slope is below 5.

options.text: H₀: β₂ = 5 against Hₐ: β₂ ≠ 5
options.feedback: This two-sided test asks whether the slope differs from 5 in either direction, not whether it exceeds 5.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 7.5: for a directional claim, put the claim in Hₐ and its opposite in H₀. A claim of 'more than 5' gives the upper-tailed test H₀: β₂ ≤ 5 vs. Hₐ: β₂ > 5.

practice.concept: One-sided p-values (Section 7.6, Key Concept 7.5)
practice.stem: An analyst claims that education raises wages by less than $3 per hour and tests H₀: β₂ ≥ 3 against Hₐ: β₂ < 3. With b₂ = 5.2 and se(b₂) = 1.8, t = 1.22. Using the normal approximation, what is the one-sided p-value?

options.text: About 0.11
options.feedback: This is the upper-tail probability. A lower-tailed test uses Pr[T < t], the area to the left of 1.22.

options.text: About 0.89
options.feedback: Correct: Pr[Z < 1.22] ≈ 0.89. The estimate lies above 3, on the wrong side of the claim, so H₀ cannot be rejected.

options.text: About 0.22
options.feedback: This is a two-sided p-value. A one-sided test uses only the tail named in Hₐ.

options.text: About 0.002
options.feedback: This uses the t statistic for H₀: β₂ = 0 (5.2 ÷ 1.8 ≈ 2.89). Here the null value is 3.

practice.explanation: Section 7.6: for a lower-tailed test, p = Pr[T < t]. With t = 1.22 > 0, p ≈ 0.89 > 0.5: when the estimate contradicts the claimed direction, a one-sided test cannot reject H₀.

practice.concept: One-sided p-values (Section 7.6, Key Concept 7.5)
practice.stem: When the slope estimate lies on the side predicted by Hₐ, the one-sided p-value is half of the two-sided p-value.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. The two-sided p-value counts both tails; the one-sided test counts only the tail in the predicted direction.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit the 'Mathematical relationship' between one-sided and two-sided p-values in Section 7.4.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 7.5: one-sided p-value = two-sided p-value ÷ 2 when the sign is as predicted. If the estimate is on the other side, the one-sided p-value exceeds 0.5.

practice.concept: Comparing classical and robust standard errors (Section 7.7)
practice.stem: Suppose a house-price regression on 100 houses gives a classical standard error of 15.0 and a heteroskedasticity-robust standard error of 22.5 for the slope. What does this suggest?

options.text: Likely heteroskedasticity; report the robust standard error.
options.feedback: Correct: a 50% gap suggests the error variance is not constant, and the classical standard error understates the uncertainty.

options.text: Little sign of a problem; report the classical standard error.
options.feedback: A 50% difference is large (the chapter flags gaps above 20%). The classical standard error is likely too small here.

options.text: A biased slope estimate; report a corrected slope instead.
options.feedback: Heteroskedasticity leaves the slope estimate unbiased; it affects the standard errors, not the coefficient.

options.text: Autocorrelated errors; report HAC standard errors.
options.feedback: HAC standard errors are for time series. These are cross-sectional data on houses.

practice.explanation: Section 7.7: when robust SEs are much larger than classical SEs, heteroskedasticity is likely and the classical t statistics are too large. Report the robust standard errors.

practice.concept: Consequences of heteroskedasticity (Section 7.7, Key Concept 7.6)
practice.stem: Suppose the errors in a cross-sectional regression are heteroskedastic, but the analyst uses default (classical) standard errors. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The R² of the regression can no longer be computed.
options.feedback: R² is computed from the residuals as usual; heteroskedasticity affects the validity of the standard errors.

options.text: The OLS slope estimate is still unbiased.
options.feedback: Correct: the coefficient estimates remain unbiased and consistent.

options.text: The default standard errors may be too small or too large.
options.feedback: Correct: the direction of the bias depends on the form of heteroskedasticity.

options.text: The reported t statistics and p-values may be misleading.
options.feedback: Correct: they are built from the wrong standard errors.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 7.6: under heteroskedasticity, b₂ is still unbiased, but default standard errors, t statistics, p-values, and confidence intervals are invalid. Robust standard errors fix the inference.

practice.concept: When to use robust standard errors (Section 7.7, Key Concept 7.6)
practice.stem: Robust standard errors should be used only after a formal test has shown that heteroskedasticity is present.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit 'Common mistakes to avoid' in Section 7.7: pre-testing is listed as a mistake.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. Robust standard errors are valid whether or not heteroskedasticity is present, so there is no need to test first.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 7.6: robust SEs are valid with or without heteroskedasticity, so modern practice reports them routinely for cross-sectional data, without pre-testing.

practice.concept: Types of robust standard errors (Section 7.7, Key Concept 7.6)
practice.stem: A researcher studies test scores of students in 200 schools, where students in the same school share unobserved influences. Which standard errors does the chapter recommend?

options.text: Classical standard errors
options.feedback: Classical standard errors assume independent, constant-variance errors, which fails when students in a school share influences.

options.text: HAC standard errors
options.feedback: HAC standard errors handle correlation over time in time series, not correlation within groups.

options.text: Cluster-robust standard errors
options.feedback: Correct: cluster-robust standard errors allow errors to be correlated within each school.

options.text: HC1 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors
options.feedback: HC1 handles non-constant variance but still treats students as independent; within-school correlation needs cluster-robust standard errors.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 7.6: HC robust SEs for cross-sections, HAC for time series, and cluster-robust SEs for grouped data such as students within schools.

exam.concept: Standard error of the slope (Sections 7.1–7.2)
exam.stem: In the Davis regression of price on size (29 houses), the slope estimate is b₂ = 73.77 with a standard error of 11.17. What does the standard error of 11.17 measure?

options.text: How far the true population slope β₂ lies from the estimate 73.77
options.feedback: The gap between b₂ and β₂ is unknown, because β₂ itself is unknown. Revisit the question a standard error answers (Section 7.2).

options.text: How much the slope estimate would typically vary across random samples of 29 houses
options.feedback: Correct. The standard error measures the sampling variability of b₂: how much it would change from one random sample to another.

options.text: How much the sizes of the 29 houses typically vary around their average size, in square feet
options.feedback: That describes the spread of one variable in the data, which is a standard deviation. Revisit the distinction drawn in Section 7.2.

options.text: How much individual sale prices typically differ from the fitted line, in dollars
options.feedback: That describes the scatter of the data around the line, measured in dollars. Revisit what the standard error of a coefficient measures (Section 7.2).

exam.explanation: Section 7.2: the standard error answers 'if we repeatedly sampled and computed b₂ each time, how much would b₂ vary?' A standard deviation describes the spread of data; a standard error describes the uncertainty of an estimate.

exam.concept: Sample estimate vs. population parameter (Sections 7.1–7.2)
exam.stem: The chapter writes the population model as price = β₁ + β₂ × size + u and reports b₂ = 73.77 for the 29 Davis houses. How are b₂ and β₂ related?

options.text: b₂ is the classical slope, and β₂ is the same slope after a heteroskedasticity adjustment.
options.feedback: Robust standard errors change the standard errors, not the slope. Revisit the notation of Section 7.1.

options.text: b₂ is the slope of the fitted line, and β₂ is its intercept.
options.feedback: Revisit how the chapter uses the subscripts and the Greek and Latin letters in Section 7.1.

options.text: b₂ equals β₂ exactly once the sample has more than 30 observations.
options.feedback: No sample size turns a sample estimate into the population value. Revisit the inference problem in Section 7.2.

options.text: b₂ is computed from the 29 houses, and it estimates the unknown population slope β₂.
options.feedback: Correct. b₂ = 73.77 is the sample estimate; β₂ is the population slope we learn about through confidence intervals and tests.

exam.explanation: Sections 7.1–7.2: Greek letters (β₁, β₂) are population parameters; Latin letters (b₁, b₂) are least-squares estimates from the sample. Statistical inference uses b₂ and se(b₂) to learn about β₂.

exam.concept: The t-distribution and degrees of freedom (Section 7.2, Key Concept 7.1)
exam.stem: Why does the chapter base inference about the slope on the t-distribution T(n − 2) rather than on the standard normal distribution?

options.text: Because the error variance σᵤ² is unknown and is replaced by an estimate
options.feedback: Correct. Replacing σᵤ with its estimate sₑ adds uncertainty, which the t-distribution accounts for.

options.text: Because house prices are skewed, and the t-distribution corrects for skewness
options.feedback: The t-distribution is symmetric, like the normal. Revisit 'Why use the T(n−2) distribution?' in Section 7.2.

options.text: Because the slope estimate b₂ is biased when the sample is small
options.feedback: Revisit the reason given under 'Why use the T(n−2) distribution?' in Section 7.2.

options.text: Because the regression has two variables, price and size, rather than one
options.feedback: The number of variables is not the reason. Revisit Key Concept 7.1 on when the t-distribution is used.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 7.1: the t-distribution is used when the population variance is unknown, which is always the case in practice. Estimating σᵤ² by sₑ² adds uncertainty, so T(n − 2) replaces N(0, 1).

exam.concept: Degrees of freedom (Section 7.2, Key Concept 7.1)
exam.stem: The Davis regression of price on size uses n = 29 houses. How many degrees of freedom does the t-distribution for the slope have?

options.text: 27, because the intercept and the slope are both estimated
options.feedback: Correct: n − 2 = 29 − 2 = 27.

options.text: 28, because one degree of freedom is lost when a mean is estimated
options.feedback: Revisit how degrees of freedom are counted for a bivariate regression (Key Concept 7.1).

options.text: 29, because every house contributes one degree of freedom
options.feedback: Revisit how estimating parameters affects the degrees of freedom (Key Concept 7.1).

options.text: 2, because the regression estimates two parameters
options.feedback: Revisit what the degrees of freedom count (Key Concept 7.1).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 7.1: start with n = 29 observations, lose one degree of freedom for the intercept and one for the slope: 29 − 2 = 27.

exam.concept: The t-distribution vs. the normal distribution (Section 7.3, Key Concept 7.1)
exam.stem: Because the t-distribution has heavier tails than the normal distribution, a 95% confidence interval for the Davis slope built with the t-distribution is narrower than one built with the normal value 1.96.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit what heavier tails imply for the critical value, and how the critical value enters the margin of error (Section 7.3).

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. Heavier tails mean a larger critical value (2.052 for the Davis regression versus 1.96), so the t-based interval is wider, by about 5%.

exam.explanation: Section 7.3: with the normal value, the margin would be 1.96 × se(b₂) ≈ 21.90; with the t-distribution, it is 2.052 × se(b₂) ≈ 22.93, about 5% wider. Heavier tails mean more conservative inference.

exam.concept: What determines the standard error of the slope (Section 7.2)
exam.stem: For the Davis regression of price on size, which changes would, other things equal, make the standard error of the slope smaller? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A larger estimated slope
options.feedback: Revisit the formula for se(b₂) in Section 7.2 and check whether the size of b₂ itself appears in it.

options.text: Collecting 116 houses instead of 29
options.feedback: Correct: more data reduce the standard error; quadrupling n roughly halves it.

options.text: Reporting a 99% instead of a 95% confidence interval
options.feedback: Revisit the difference between the standard error and the confidence level (Sections 7.2–7.3).

options.text: Sampling houses with a wider range of sizes
options.feedback: Correct: more spread in x gives more information about the slope.

options.text: Prices that lie closer to the fitted line
options.feedback: Correct: less unexplained variation (smaller sₑ) gives a more precise slope.

exam.explanation: Section 7.2: se(b₂) = sₑ / √Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² falls with less scatter around the line, more observations, and a wider spread in x. The size of b₂ and the confidence level do not enter it.

exam.concept: Standard error formula (Section 7.2)
exam.stem: Suppose the Davis houses had been sampled with twice the spread in size, so that the standard deviation of size were about 796 square feet instead of 398, with n = 29 and sₑ ≈ 23,551 dollars unchanged. Using the chapter's shortcut formula, what would the standard error of the slope be, approximately?

options.text: About 29.6
options.feedback: Revisit the shortcut formula in Section 7.2 and check how each of the three ingredients enters it.

options.text: About 1.0
options.feedback: Revisit the shortcut formula in Section 7.2 and check how each of the three ingredients enters it.

options.text: About 5.5
About 22.0
options.feedback: Revisit how the spread of x affects the standard error (Section 7.2).

exam.explanation: se(b₂) ≈ sₑ / (√n × sₓ) = 23,551 / (√29 × 796) ≈ 23,551 / 4,287 ≈ 5.5. Doubling the spread of x halves the standard error.

exam.concept: Constructing a confidence interval (Section 7.3)
exam.stem: For the Davis slope, b₂ = 73.77 and se(b₂) = 11.17. The critical value for a 90% confidence interval with this sample is 1.703. What is the 90% confidence interval for β₂?

options.feedback: Revisit how the margin of error is built for a given confidence level (Section 7.3).
This interval is implausibly narrow for an estimate whose standard error is 11.17. Revisit the margin-of-error formula (Section 7.3).
Revisit the margin-of-error formula and recompute it step by step (Section 7.3).

exam.explanation: Section 7.3: CI = b₂ ± t-critical × se(b₂) = 73.77 ± 1.703 × 11.17 = 73.77 ± 19.02 = [54.75, 92.79]. It is narrower than the 95% interval [50.84, 96.70] because 90% confidence uses a smaller critical value.

exam.concept: Interpreting confidence intervals (Section 7.3, Key Concept 7.2)
exam.stem: If 100 different random samples of 29 Davis houses were each used to build a 95% confidence interval for the slope, we would expect about 5 of those intervals to miss the true slope β₂.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. The 95% is the long-run success rate of the procedure, so about 5 in 100 intervals miss β₂ just by chance.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit the 'CORRECT' interpretation in Key Concept 7.2.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 7.2: the randomness is in the sampling process. About 95 of 100 such intervals contain β₂; any single interval, such as [50.84, 96.70], either contains it or does not.

exam.concept: Interpreting confidence intervals (Section 7.3, Key Concept 7.2)
exam.stem: The 95% confidence interval for the Davis slope is [50.84, 96.70] dollars per square foot. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: About 95% of the 29 houses sold for between $50.84 and $96.70 per square foot.
options.feedback: Revisit what the interval is about: a population parameter or individual houses (Key Concept 7.2).

options.text: A 99% interval from the same data would be wider than this one.
options.feedback: Correct: higher confidence requires a larger critical value.

options.text: If the standard error were twice as large, with all else unchanged, the interval would be twice as wide.
options.feedback: Correct: the width is 2 × t-critical × se(b₂), proportional to the standard error.

options.text: A true slope of $40 per square foot is impossible, since 40 lies outside the interval.
options.feedback: Revisit what being outside a 95% interval does and does not imply (Key Concept 7.2).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 7.2: the interval concerns β₂, not individual houses. Its width, 2 × t-critical × se(b₂), grows with the confidence level and the standard error. Values outside are implausible at the 95% level, not impossible.

exam.concept: Margin of error (Section 7.3)
exam.stem: The 95% confidence interval for the Davis slope is [50.84, 96.70]. What is its margin of error?

options.feedback: Revisit the definition of the margin of error in the chapter's Key Concepts and Section 7.3.
This number is the center of the interval. Revisit the definition of the margin of error (Section 7.3).
Revisit the difference between the standard error and the margin of error (Section 7.3).
Correct: the margin is the half-width, (96.70 − 50.84) ÷ 2 = 22.93, the critical value 2.052 times the standard error.

exam.explanation: The margin of error is the half-width of the interval, t-critical × se(b₂) with t-critical = 2.052; the interval is 73.77 ± 22.93.

exam.concept: Comparing confidence intervals (Section 7.3, Key Concept 7.2)
exam.stem: Suppose a study of houses in another town reports a slope of $75 per square foot with a 95% confidence interval of [5, 145]. Compared with the Davis interval [50.84, 96.70], which conclusion is correct?

options.text: The other town's slope is more precise, because its interval covers more values.
options.feedback: Revisit what the width of a confidence interval says about precision (Key Concept 7.2).

options.text: The two slopes are equally precise, because the point estimates are so similar.
options.feedback: Revisit which feature of an interval reflects precision (Key Concept 7.2).

options.text: The other town's slope is not significantly different from zero at the 5% level.
options.feedback: Check this premise against the interval reported for the other town (Section 7.5).

options.text: The Davis slope is estimated more precisely, because its interval is narrower.
options.feedback: Correct. The Davis interval is about 46 wide versus 140 for the other town.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 7.2: narrower intervals mean more precision. Both intervals exclude zero, so both slopes are significant at 5%, but the Davis interval (width ≈ 46) is far narrower than [5, 145] (width 140).

exam.concept: The artificial-data example (Section 7.4, Key Concept 7.1)
exam.stem: In the chapter's artificial example with only n = 5 observations, the slope estimate is 0.40 and the 95% confidence interval is [0.03, 0.77]. Which explanation for the interval's width is correct?

options.text: The interval is wide because, with only five observations, the critical value is 3.182.
options.feedback: Correct: with so few observations the t critical value is 3.182, and 3.182 × 0.115 ≈ 0.37 is almost as large as the estimate.

options.text: The interval is wide because the slope is not statistically significant at the 5% level.
options.feedback: Check this premise against the interval itself before using it as an explanation (Section 7.4).

options.text: The interval is wide because the slope estimate of 0.40 is small in absolute terms.
options.feedback: Revisit what determines the width of a confidence interval (Section 7.3).

options.text: The interval is wide because artificial data are less reliable than data from real markets.
options.feedback: Revisit the factors that set the width of a confidence interval (Section 7.3).

exam.explanation: Section 7.4 (artificial data): with n = 5 the critical value jumps to 3.182, so the margin 3.182 × se(b₂) ≈ 3.182 × 0.115 ≈ 0.37 nearly equals the slope 0.40, a concrete illustration of how small samples inflate the margin of error.

exam.concept: Interpreting p-values (Section 7.4, Key Concept 7.3)
exam.stem: For the Davis slope, the two-sided p-value for H₀: β₂ = 0 is below 0.001. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: There is less than a 0.1% probability that the true population slope β₂ is exactly equal to zero.
options.feedback: Revisit what a p-value is a probability of (Key Concept 7.3).

options.text: There is a more than 99.9% probability that the slope estimate of 73.77 is exactly the right value.
options.feedback: Revisit what a p-value measures (Key Concept 7.3).

options.text: If β₂ were zero, an estimate at least as far from zero as 73.77 would arise in under 0.1% of samples.
options.feedback: Correct. The p-value is computed assuming H₀ is true: such an extreme estimate would be very rare if size had no linear relationship with price.

options.text: Fewer than 0.1% of the 29 houses in the sample lie far away from the fitted regression line.
options.feedback: Revisit what the p-value refers to (Key Concept 7.3).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 7.3: the p-value is the probability, if H₀ were true, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed. It is not the probability that H₀ is true.

exam.concept: Tests of statistical significance (Section 7.4)
exam.stem: For the same 29 Davis houses, a regression of price on the number of bedrooms gives a slope of $23,667 per bedroom with a standard error of $9,638. The two-sided critical values are 2.052 at the 5% level and 2.771 at the 1% level. What do you conclude about H₀: β₂ = 0?

options.text: Reject H₀ at both the 5% and the 1% level
options.feedback: Compute the t statistic and compare it with each critical value in turn (Section 7.4).

options.text: Reject H₀ at the 5% level but not at the 1% level
options.feedback: Correct: t = 23,667 ÷ 9,638 ≈ 2.46, above 2.052 but below 2.771.

options.text: Reject H₀ at neither the 5% nor the 1% level
options.feedback: Recompute the t statistic and compare it with both critical values (Section 7.4).

options.text: Reject H₀ at the 1% level but not at the 5% level
options.feedback: A result that is significant at the 1% level is also significant at the 5% level. Revisit the decision rules in Section 7.4.

exam.explanation: Section 7.4: t = b₂ / se(b₂) = 23,667 / 9,638 ≈ 2.46 (p ≈ 0.02). Since 2.052 < 2.46 < 2.771, the number of bedrooms is significant at the 5% level but not at the 1% level.

exam.concept: The hypothesis testing framework (Section 7.4, Key Concept 7.3)
exam.stem: A researcher tests H₀: β₂ = 0 against Hₐ: β₂ ≠ 0 for the Davis slope at the 5% significance level. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: If H₀ were true, this test would wrongly reject it 5% of the time.
options.feedback: Correct: α is the probability of a Type I error.

options.text: The null hypothesis is the claim the researcher hopes to establish.
options.feedback: Revisit the roles of the null and the alternative hypotheses (Key Concept 7.3).

options.text: A smaller p-value means a larger estimated slope.
options.feedback: Revisit what the p-value measures (Key Concept 7.3).

options.text: If |t| exceeds the critical value of 2.052, H₀ is rejected at the 5% level.
options.feedback: Correct: this is the critical-value decision rule.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 7.3: H₀ is usually 'no effect' and Hₐ is what we conclude if H₀ is rejected; α is the Type I error probability; reject if p < α or, equivalently, if |t| > t-critical. A p-value reflects the estimate relative to its standard error, not the estimate alone.

exam.concept: Economic magnitude of the slope (Section 7.4, Key Concept 7.4)
exam.stem: Using the Davis slope of $73.77 per square foot, how much higher is the predicted price of a house that is 200 square feet larger than another house?

options.feedback: Revisit how the slope turns a difference in size into a difference in predicted price (Key Concept 7.4).
Revisit what a difference between two predicted prices depends on (Section 7.4).
Revisit how the slope turns a difference in size into a difference in predicted price (Key Concept 7.4).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 7.4: economic significance is judged from the magnitude of b₂. A 200 sq ft difference predicts 200 × 73.77 = $14,754 more, a substantial amount in a market where the average house sold for about $254,000.

exam.concept: Statistical vs. economic significance (Section 7.4, Key Concept 7.4)
exam.stem: The Davis slope is highly statistically significant (p < 0.001). What additional question does economic significance ask?

options.text: Whether the p-value is also below the stricter 1% level
options.feedback: That is still a question about statistical significance. Revisit Key Concept 7.4.

options.text: Whether the t statistic exceeds the critical value
options.feedback: That is the critical-value version of the significance test itself. Revisit Key Concept 7.4.

options.text: Whether the sample has more than 30 observations
options.feedback: Sample size affects statistical precision. Revisit what economic significance is about (Key Concept 7.4).

options.text: Whether about $74 per square foot matters in practice
options.feedback: Correct. Economic significance asks whether the magnitude of the effect is large enough to matter in real-world terms.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 7.4: statistical significance asks whether the effect differs from zero; economic significance asks whether it is large enough to matter, judged from the magnitude of b₂ and the context.

exam.concept: Statistical significance of the intercept (Section 7.4, Key Concept 7.4)
exam.stem: The intercept of the Davis regression is $115,017 with p < 0.001. Which interpretation is best?

options.text: It is significant, so an empty lot in Davis is worth about $115,017 on average.
options.feedback: Nothing in this regression measures land values. Revisit what the intercept represents in this regression.

options.text: It is not meaningful, because its standard error exceeds the slope's.
options.feedback: The two standard errors are measured in different units, so comparing them says nothing. Revisit Key Concept 7.4.

options.text: It is significant, but it predicts the price at 0 sq ft, far outside the observed data.
options.feedback: Correct. No house has zero square feet (sizes range from 1,400 to 3,300), so a significant intercept need not be economically meaningful.

options.text: It is the key result, because it is the largest coefficient in the regression.
options.feedback: The size of a coefficient depends on its units. Revisit Key Concept 7.4.

exam.explanation: Statistical significance does not make a number economically meaningful. The intercept is the predicted price when size = 0, far outside the observed 1,400–3,300 sq ft range; the slope is the number of interest.

exam.concept: Statistical vs. economic significance (Section 7.4, Key Concept 7.4)
exam.stem: Suppose a study of 100,000 house sales estimates a slope of just $0.06 per square foot with a standard error of $0.02. Although economically trivial, this slope is statistically significant at the 1% level.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. t = 0.06 ÷ 0.02 = 3.0, above the 1% critical value (about 2.58 with this many observations): with very large samples, even an economically trivial slope can be statistically significant.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit how the sample size affects the standard error and the t statistic, and compute t here (Key Concept 7.4).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 7.4: with large n, even tiny effects become statistically significant. Statistical significance is not economic significance.

exam.concept: Two-sided test of a specific value (Section 7.5)
exam.stem: For the Davis slope (b₂ = 73.77, se(b₂) = 11.17), what is the t statistic for testing H₀: β₂ = 100 against Hₐ: β₂ ≠ 100?

options.feedback: Revisit the formula for the t statistic in Section 7.5 and recompute.
Revisit the formula for the t statistic in Section 7.5 and recompute.
Revisit the formula for the t statistic in Section 7.5 and recompute.

exam.explanation: Section 7.5: t = (b₂ − β₂*) / se(b₂) = (73.77 − 100) / 11.17 ≈ −2.35. Since |−2.35| > 2.052, H₀: β₂ = 100 is rejected at the 5% level, consistent with 100 lying outside the 95% interval.

exam.concept: Confidence intervals and two-sided tests (Section 7.5, Key Concept 7.2)
exam.stem: The 95% confidence interval for the Davis slope is [50.84, 96.70]. For which hypothesized values c would a two-sided test of H₀: β₂ = c be rejected at the 5% level? (Select all that apply.)

options.feedback: Correct: 45 lies below the lower limit 50.84.
Compare this value carefully with the interval's endpoints (Section 7.5).
Revisit how the confidence interval relates to two-sided tests (Section 7.5).
Compare this value carefully with the interval's endpoints (Section 7.5).
Correct: 99 lies above the upper limit 96.70.

exam.explanation: Section 7.5: a 5% two-sided test rejects H₀: β₂ = c exactly when c lies outside the 95% interval. Only 45 and 99 lie outside [50.84, 96.70] (t ≈ 2.57 and −2.26).

exam.concept: Interpreting a failure to reject (Sections 7.4–7.5)
exam.stem: Because the two-sided test of H₀: β₂ = 90 is not rejected at the 5% level, the Davis data show that the true slope equals $90 per square foot.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit what 'fail to reject' means: many other values are also consistent with the data (Section 7.5).

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. Failing to reject means 90 is consistent with the data, as is every value inside the confidence interval; we never 'accept' H₀.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 7.3: we never accept H₀, we only fail to reject it. The data are consistent with β₂ = 90, but also with 60, 75, and every other value in [50.84, 96.70].

exam.concept: When to use a one-sided test (Section 7.6, Key Concept 7.5)
exam.stem: In which situation does the chapter consider a one-sided test of the slope appropriate?

options.text: When a two-sided test narrowly fails to reject H₀ and the researcher wants a significant result
options.feedback: Revisit the cautions about one-sided tests in Key Concept 7.5 and Section 7.4.

options.text: When the estimated slope turns out to have the sign the researcher hoped for
options.feedback: Revisit the conditions listed under 'When to use one-sided tests' (Key Concept 7.5).

options.text: When theory predicts the direction of the effect before the data are examined
options.feedback: Correct. A one-sided test is justified by a directional prediction made before seeing the data.

options.text: When the sample has fewer than 30 observations
options.feedback: Sample size bears on the t versus normal choice, not on one- versus two-sided tests. Revisit Key Concept 7.5.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 7.5: use a one-sided test only with a strong theoretical prediction of direction made before seeing the data. Switching to one-sided after seeing results is fishing; two-sided tests are the standard.

exam.concept: One-sided p-values (Section 7.6, Key Concept 7.5)
exam.stem: To test the claim that each square foot adds less than $90, the chapter runs the lower-tailed test H₀: β₂ ≥ 90 against Hₐ: β₂ < 90, using b₂ = 73.77. The two-sided p-value for H₀: β₂ = 90 is 0.158. What are the one-sided p-value and the conclusion?

options.text: p = 0.158: do not reject H₀ at the 5% level, and do not reject it at the 10% level
options.feedback: Revisit how a one-sided p-value relates to the two-sided one (Key Concept 7.5).

options.text: p = 0.316: do not reject H₀ at the 5% level, and do not reject it at the 10% level
options.feedback: Revisit the relationship between one-sided and two-sided p-values (Section 7.6).

options.text: p = 0.079: do not reject H₀ at the 5% level, but reject it at the 10% level
options.feedback: Correct: the estimate is on the side predicted by Hₐ, so the one-sided p-value is 0.158 ÷ 2 = 0.079, between 0.05 and 0.10.

options.text: p = 0.921: do not reject H₀ at the 5% level or at any other conventional level
options.feedback: Revisit how a one-sided p-value relates to the two-sided one (Key Concept 7.5).

exam.explanation: Section 7.6: with t ≈ −1.45, Pr[T₂₇ < −1.45] = 0.079, half the two-sided p-value. There is not enough evidence at 5% that β₂ < 90, but there would be at 10%.

exam.concept: Direction in one-sided tests (Section 7.6, Key Concept 7.5)
exam.stem: With b₂ = 73.77, an upper-tailed test of H₀: β₂ ≤ 80 against Hₐ: β₂ > 80 cannot reject H₀ at any conventional significance level.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. The estimate lies below 80, on the side of the null, so the one-sided p-value exceeds 0.5 (about 0.71).

options.text: False
options.feedback: Check on which side of 80 the estimate lies, and what that implies for an upper-tailed test (Key Concept 7.5).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 7.5: if the data contradict the predicted direction, a one-sided test cannot reject H₀ (p > 0.5). Here t = (73.77 − 80)/11.17 ≈ −0.56 and Pr[T₂₇ > −0.56] ≈ 0.71.

exam.concept: Why use robust standard errors (Section 7.7, Key Concept 7.6)
exam.stem: Why does the chapter recommend heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors for cross-sectional data such as the Davis houses?

options.text: They make the error variance constant across all the observations.
options.feedback: Robust standard errors do not change the errors themselves. Revisit what they adjust (Key Concept 7.6).

options.text: They remain valid even if the spread of the errors changes with house size.
options.feedback: Correct. They do not rely on the constant-variance assumption, so they are free insurance against heteroskedasticity.

options.text: They are designed for data observed over time, such as quarterly GDP.
options.feedback: Revisit the types of robust standard errors and the data each one is designed for (Key Concept 7.6).

options.text: They ensure that the slope measures the causal effect of size on price.
options.feedback: Standard errors concern the precision of an estimate, not causation. Revisit Key Concept 7.6.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 7.6: heteroskedasticity-robust SEs are valid whether or not the error variance is constant, so they are modern best practice for cross-sectional data, with no need to test for heteroskedasticity first.

exam.concept: Comparing classical and robust standard errors (Section 7.7)
exam.stem: Re-estimating the Davis regression with heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) standard errors raises the slope's standard error from 11.17 to 11.33, and the 95% confidence interval becomes [50.52, 97.02] instead of [50.84, 96.70]. Which conclusions are supported? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The slope estimate itself is unchanged at 73.77.
options.feedback: Correct: robust methods change only the standard errors, t statistics, p-values, and intervals.

options.text: The robust t statistic for size is larger than the classical one.
options.feedback: Revisit how a change in the standard error moves the t statistic (Section 7.7).

options.text: Size remains statistically significant at the 5% level.
options.feedback: Correct: the robust interval still excludes zero.

options.text: The robust interval is slightly wider than the classical one.
options.feedback: Correct: a larger standard error gives a slightly wider interval (46.5 versus 45.9).

exam.explanation: Section 7.7: the coefficient stays at 73.77; the robust SE is 1.4% larger, so the robust t (6.51) is slightly smaller than the classical t (6.60), and the conclusions do not change.

exam.concept: Robust vs. classical standard errors (Section 7.7, Key Concept 7.6)
exam.stem: Heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors are always at least as large as the corresponding classical standard errors.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit 'Case 3' in Section 7.7 and the Davis comparison table of standard and robust SEs.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. Robust SEs are usually larger but can be smaller: in the Davis regression, the intercept's robust SE (20,299) is below its classical SE (21,489).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 7.6: robust SEs are usually larger (more conservative) but sometimes smaller. In the Davis regression, the slope's SE rises 1.4% while the intercept's falls 5.5%.

exam.concept: Detecting heteroskedasticity (Section 7.7)
exam.stem: In a plot of the residuals against the fitted values, which pattern suggests heteroskedasticity?

options.text: The vertical spread of the residuals widens as the fitted values of price increase.
options.feedback: Correct. A funnel shape means the error variance changes with the fitted values.

options.text: The residuals scatter randomly around zero with the same spread everywhere.
options.feedback: Revisit which residual pattern the chapter associates with constant variance (Section 7.7).

options.text: Roughly half of the residuals are positive and half are negative.
options.feedback: Revisit what the residual plot is used to check (Section 7.7).

options.text: The residuals average to zero across the whole range of fitted values.
options.feedback: Revisit what feature of the residual plot reveals non-constant variance (Section 7.7).

exam.explanation: Section 7.7: homoskedasticity shows as random scatter with constant spread; heteroskedasticity shows as a funnel, with spread that widens or narrows across fitted values.
